analysis.one_liner: Shielded the President from money-damages lawsuits while in office and made taxpayers pay his legal fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors until the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred any civil lawsuit seeking money damages against the sitting President — for conduct before or during the term — until 180 days after leaving office. While the President was shielded, the clock on those claims would be paused, not erased. If the President won such a case, the Treasury Department would reimburse his attorney's fees, and courts could sanction people who filed suits the judge deemed improper.
analysis.who_benefits: The sitting President, and former Presidents facing suits over conduct from their term. They would be untouchable in money-damages suits for years at a time — even for personal, non-official conduct — and taxpayers would cover their legal bills whenever they prevailed.

how_it_helps.text: Grants the President immunity from all civil suits seeking money damages from taking office until 180 days after leaving, covering causes of action that arose before or during the term.
Pauses the statute of limitations during the immunity period, so plaintiffs' claims survive but are delayed rather than extinguished.
Directs the Treasury to reimburse the President or former President for reasonable attorney's fees and costs whenever he gets a suit dismissed under the immunity or otherwise prevails.
Lets courts sanction plaintiffs or their attorneys — including ordering them to repay the Treasury — for suits deemed unfounded or brought to harass.

analysis.who_pays: People with legitimate damages claims against a President would have to wait out the immunity window — potentially years — before their day in court. Taxpayers would pay the President's attorney's fees in any case he won. And the sanctions provision could discourage people from bringing suits at all.

drawbacks.text: The immunity covers all civil damages suits, not just suits over official acts, so personal conduct from before or during the term would be shielded while the President held office.
A person with a valid claim would have to wait until 180 days after the President left office — and any subsequent appeals — to have it heard, since the limitations clock is merely paused.
Taxpayers, not the President personally, would fund his legal defense through Treasury reimbursements whenever he prevailed.
The sanctions provision, allowing penalties against plaintiffs whose suits are judged not 'well grounded in fact,' could deter people with genuine claims from suing a current or former President.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's defenders could point to a real concern: a President distracted or harassed by personal damages litigation while running the country. But the design goes well beyond that — it shields even pre-term personal conduct, shifts the President's legal bills to taxpayers, and adds sanctions that could scare off legitimate plaintiffs. The cost to accountability for the nation's most powerful officeholder outweighs the convenience to the officeholder.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1994, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee three weeks later, and then sat there until the Congress ended in January 1995 — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Rose introduced the Presidential Immunity Act of 1994 on August 12, 1994, near the end of the 103rd Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On September 21, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration.
No further action was taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill died in subcommittee without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing rule — that a President can be sued for money damages like anyone else — stayed in place, preserving accountability for the office. Plaintiffs and the public came out ahead; the only thing spared a President was litigation risk he already faces under current law.

for.name: Rep. Charlie Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so no partisan pattern in support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted Presidents from money-damages suits for years at a time and made taxpayers cover their legal fees when they won. That gain comes directly at the expense of people with legitimate claims and of public accountability for the office.
